title: AI Errors and Graceful Failure
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: AI Errors and Graceful Failure.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Probabilistic systems can be wrong without looking broken. They can produce a plausible fabrication, omit a decisive fact, apply a rule outside its context, retrieve stale information, misread ambiguous input, call the wrong tool, or execute a valid action with the wrong permission. People may not detect these failures because fluency and interface polish remain intact.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Design the failure, not only the ideal output
turns.text: What changes when we look at design the failure, not only the ideal output?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Graceful failure therefore has four jobs:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: 1. Limit consequence: prevent or contain unsafe action. 2. Make state legible: distinguish known, inferred, missing, stale, and failed information. 3. Preserve progress: retain valid input, selections, and context. 4. Provide a changed route: clarify, verify, use an authoritative source, switch method, escalate, reverse, or appeal.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An apology is not recovery. “Try again” is not a changed route when the same boundary will persist.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at build a system-level failure taxonomy?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Do not label every problem “the AI was wrong.” Locate where the experience can fail:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Input: ambiguous, incomplete, conflicting, out of scope, malicious, or inaccessible. Data and retrieval: absent, stale, duplicated, unauthorised, poorly ranked, or from the wrong source. Model: misclassification, hallucination, unstable generation, bias, or weak generalisation. Policy: unclear or conflicting rules; unsafe request accepted; safe request blocked.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Tool and integration: wrong API call, timeout, partial write, duplicate action, or stale state. Permission: data or action exceeds the person’s delegation contract. Interface interpretation: provenance, uncertainty, or role is misunderstood. Human workflow: reviewer overload, bad escalation, missing authority, or delayed response.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Downstream outcome: a technically valid output creates harm in the real service.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: For each failure, record trigger, detection signal, affected people, consequence, reversibility, safe state, user message, preserved context, recovery route, escalation, owner, and learning path. Treat false positives and false negatives separately; their harms and safeguards often differ.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at abstention is a product capability?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A mature system can decide that available evidence is insufficient for a dependable output. Abstention should be specific and useful:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: say what cannot be established; identify the missing or conflicting evidence; request one answer that can genuinely resolve ambiguity; narrow the task to a part the system can support; present authoritative source material without inventing a conclusion; offer a human or deterministic route with expectations; preserve everything already entered.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Avoid treating low model confidence as the only trigger. A high-confidence output may still concern a prohibited action, stale source, unfamiliar population, or severe consequence. Conversely, uncertainty does not always require stopping; a low-risk draft can remain useful when clearly editable.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at preserve truth during partial action?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Agentic and integrated systems can fail midway. The interface must distinguish planned, started, completed, confirmed, reversed, and unresolved actions. Never infer success from a request being sent. Use idempotent operations where possible so retrying does not duplicate a booking or referral.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Show the person what changed, what did not, and what remains uncertain. A rollback may not erase a message already received or data already disclosed; describe residual effects honestly. Where reversal is impossible, provide remediation and accountable support rather than a decorative undo control.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Feedback and recourse serve different needs
turns.text: What changes when we look at feedback and recourse serve different needs?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Feedback helps improve a system. Recourse helps the affected person obtain correction or remedy now. Do not replace one with the other.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Useful feedback captures the relevant output, model/data version, source state, user correction, context, and consequence—subject to minimisation and permission. Let people add context without requiring technical diagnosis. Explain whether feedback affects their present case, future systems, or neither.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Recourse must reach a role with authority, have a response expectation, preserve evidence, and allow the outcome to change. High-severity incidents may require proactive notification, service recovery, regulatory processes, or support for people who never used the interface themselves.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: ai writing assistant?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A writing tool cannot verify a cited statistic. Rather than fabricate a source or repeatedly regenerate, it should retain the draft, mark the unsupported sentence, offer to remove or rephrase the claim, and let the writer search an authoritative source.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The consequence is lower than a clinical referral, so human review is usually enough; the same recovery pattern is calibrated to a different risk.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Confident fabrication: uncertainty or missing evidence becomes fluent fact. Retry loop: repeated generation produces variation without a safer route. Context loss: failure removes input, comparison, or work needed to recover. False success: an initiated external action is presented as completed.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: One generic fallback: every failure routes to the same apology or overloaded support queue. Feedback void: reports disappear without helping the affected person or responsible team. Recourse theatre: review exists but cannot change the outcome. User-as-debugger: people must classify technical errors or repeatedly reproduce sensitive cases.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior practitioners budget for failure as part of the product, service, and operating model. They define severity, incident ownership, response times, fallback capacity, evidence retention, affected-person communication, and post-incident learning before launch.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: They test harmful but plausible outputs, compound failures, load, staff absence, vendor outages, and policy conflicts—not merely an amusing hallucination.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: They also make failure visible upstream. If recurring recovery depends on heroic human intervention, the feature is externalising its true cost onto operations and users.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a route-planning assistant. When live transit data is unavailable, the assistant should not invent an arrival time. It can state what is stale, show the last verified schedule, offer a direct timetable, and suggest checking the operator. Graceful failure preserves the person's ability to act even when the model cannot answer.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Cause a low-stakes AI product to fail or refuse. Does it name the actual boundary? Is your work preserved? Does the next action change the conditions of success? Can you distinguish feedback from help with your current outcome? If repeated generation is the main recovery, the product has delegated error handling to you.
